content.thinking:
I'm checking the claims one by one. The root cause holds up: requests rose and CPU hit its limit, and the record confirms that requests queued for CPU. The plain-words version of the cause is supported too. The part still at risk is what I'm turning to next.

I'm going through the remaining claims: the symptom of slowed shop pages holds up against the series, the p95 rise is backed by the same lines, and the several-fold request increase and in-step CPU rise both check out. I'm now looking at the autoscaling point, where the record shows three replicas throughout and no automatic additions, while the values file only contains the settings.

I'm checking whether "no person was engaged" goes beyond what the record shows: it confirms nobody was paged and no on-call incident was linked, but it doesn't rule out someone seeing the Slack post.

I'm now questioning whether "no person was engaged" is supported, since the record only shows nobody was paged, while Argus did post to Slack. I'll keep the "nobody was paged" part and flag the engagement claim as one the record doesn't establish.

flags.why: The record says only that nobody was paged and that Argus posted about the incident in Slack; it does not establish that no person engaged with it.

supported.quote: Requests to io-shop climbed from {R1.1} to as high as {R1.3}, and CPU use climbed with them until it reached the service's CPU limit ({R2.3} at its highest).
From then on the replicas had more work than CPU to do it, so requests waited for CPU and responses slowed.
rows: The record confirmed [C1]: the load outgrew the CPU the service had

supported.quote: The shop got far more requests than usual, more than its servers had the computing power to handle at once, so requests had to wait their turn.
rows: The record confirmed [C1]: the load outgrew the CPU the service had

supported.quote: Shop pages slowed sharply for shoppers
Responses from io-shop slowed sharply. The time within which nearly all requests are answered rose far above its usual level, so shoppers waited much longer for pages.
Requests were waiting for CPU: the service was using all of the CPU its limit allowed.
rows: The record confirmed [C1]: the load outgrew the CPU the service had

supported.quote: CPU use reached that limit because requests rose to several times their level before the onset and CPU use rose in step with them. That was more load than the replicas' CPU could handle.
rows: The record confirmed [C1]: the load outgrew the CPU the service had

supported.quote: No replicas were seen being added automatically as CPU use reached its limit. The service stayed at {T20.2} replicas until Argus scaled it out.

Each request likely cost more CPU than it needed to. Code-Fix read the files behind the account page's spending figures: the default figure, and the one behind typical-purchase-feature, both do work that grows with the square of a shopper's purchase history. Nothing has run this reading.
No alert was seen when CPU use neared its limit. The slowdown was found only by the latency alert, which waits {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires.
Nobody was paged: the alert did not open an on-call incident
rows: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one.
